question: Two cyclists, \(k\) miles apart, and starting at the same time, would be together in \(r\) hours if they traveled in the same direction, but would pass each other in \(t\) hours if they traveled in opposite directions. The ratio of the speed of the faster cyclist to that of the slower is:
solution:
The gap closes at the difference of the speeds when the cyclists travel in the same direction, and at their sum when they travel toward each other. Let their constant speeds be \(u>v>0\) miles per hour, with initial separation \(k>0\) miles. Since each trip closes the same gap,
\[
r(u-v)=k=t(u+v).
\]
Also, \(u+v>u-v>0\), so
\[
t=\frac{k}{u+v}<\frac{k}{u-v}=r.
\]
Thus \(r-t\) is positive. Expanding the common-gap equation and collecting terms gives
\[
ru-rv=tu+tv,
\qquad
(r-t)u=(r+t)v.
\]
Dividing by the nonzero quantity \((r-t)v\), we obtain the requested ratio
\[
\frac{u}{v}=\frac{r+t}{r-t},
\]
choice A.
